name: walkthrough
title: Implementing a Lambda Calculus Reducer
description: Build a complete lambda calculus reducer: AST nodes (Var, Lam, App), free_vars, capture-avoiding substitute, normal-order and applicative-order reduction, step tracer, REPL, Y combinator, and SKI combinatory logic.

steps.description: Part 1: AST for lambda calculus with Var, Lam, App classes and convenience constructors.
Var: frozen dataclass with name field, __str__ returns the name.
Lam: abstraction with name and body, __str__ prints as λname. body.
App: application with func and arg, __str__ prints as (func arg).
Convenience constructors: var, lam, app for easy AST building.
Examples: identity, true_, false_ demonstrate AST construction and printing.
Move to Block 5: is_redex and beta_step functions.
Redex detection and beta reduction.
Is_redex: checks if term is App of Lam (a redex).
Beta_step: contracts a redex by substituting arg into lam body.
Tests: (λx. x x) y -> y y and (λx. x) z -> z.

steps.question: What does beta_step(redex) output for (λx. x x) y?

steps.description: Move to Block 6: normal-order reduction.
Normal-order step and reduce functions.
Normal_order_step: finds leftmost outermost redex, contracts it, or recurses left-to-right.
Leftmost first: tries function before argument in App.
Reduce under lambdas: normal order reduces inside lambda bodies.
Reduce_normal: iterates normal_order_step with trace and step limit.
Move to Block 8: applicative-order reduction.
Applicative-order step and reduce functions.
Applicative_order_step: reduces arguments first (innermost), then contracts redex.
Reduce arguments first: fully reduces func and arg before contracting.
Reduce under lambdas: applicative order also reduces inside bodies.
Reduce_applicative: iterates with trace and step limit, prints warning on divergence.
Move to Block 9: REPL for interactive reduction.
REPL that parses input, reduces with chosen strategy, shows result and free variables.
Repl_lc: reads lines, parses with parse_lc, reduces with selected strategy.
Move to Block 10: Named recursive baseline for factorial.
Named factorial function as baseline.
Recursive definition: factorial_named calls itself by name.
Test: prints factorial for range(8).

steps.question: What does print([factorial_named(n) for n in range(8)]) output?

steps.description: Move to Block 11: Step 1, pass a copy of yourself.
First step toward anonymous recursion: receive self as argument.
Step1: lambda self: lambda n: recursive logic with self(self)(n-1).
Bootstrap: factorial_v1 = step1(step1) passes function to itself.
Verification: prints factorial_v1(5) and factorial_v1(7).
Move to Block 12: Step 2, cleaning up the body.
Step2: wrap self-application in rec to hide machinery.
Step2: outer lambda self, inner lambda rec wraps the logic, immediately called.
Clean body: lambda n: 1 if n == 0 else n * rec(n - 1).
Key insight: rec = lambda n: self(self)(n) hides the self-application.
Move to Block 13: Step 3, separating logic from fixed-point machinery.
Y_machinery: separates generator from fixed-point logic.
Factorial_generator: lambda rec: lambda n: the pure logic without machinery.
Y_machinery: the fixed-point operator that works for ANY generator.
Generalization: Y_machinery works for factorial and fib generators.
Move to Block 14: Haskell Y combinator.
Haskell Y combinator with laziness.
Definition: y f = let x = f x in x, lazily evaluated.
Usage: factorial = fix (ec n -> if n == 0 then 1 else n * rec (n-1)).
Move to Block 15: Fixed point illustration.
Fixed point of cos and Z combinator verification.
Fixed_point: iteratively finds x where f(x) = x.
Verification: cos fixed point is approximately 0.7390851332.
Z combinator: same fixed point property verified for factorial.

steps.question: What does print(f"Fixed point of cos: {fp_cos:.10f}") output?

steps.description: Move to Block 16: Y Without Y - fixed-point tricks.
Alternative fixed-point patterns without explicit Y.
Default argument hack: exploits Python eager default binding.
Move to Block 17: Combinatory logic setup.
Combinatory logic introduction.
Readiness: print('Ready to meet the flock.').
Move to Block 18: Identity Bird I.
Identity bird I.
I: lambda a: a, passes argument unchanged.
Tests: I(42), I('hello'), I(I)(42) all work.
Move to Block 19: Kestrel K.
Kestrel K and KI.
Definitions: I and K defined.
K tests: K('first')('second') returns 'first'.
KI: K(I) behaves as Church false, returns second argument.
Move to Block 20: Bluebird B.
Bluebird B and B from SKI.
Definitions: K, S, B.
Examples: double and add_one functions.
Composition: B(add_one)(double)(5) = 11, B(double)(add_one)(5) = 12.
Move to Block 21: Cardinal C.
Cardinal C and C from SKI.
Definitions: K, S, B, C.
Flip: C(subtract)(10)(3) = -7 instead of 7.
Derivation: C = S(BBS)(KK), verified.
Move to Block 22: Starling S.
Starling S and its power.
Definitions: K and S.
Succ: S(add)(K(1)) creates successor function.
Move to Block 23: Mockingbird M.
Mockingbird M (self-application).
M: lambda a: a(a), applies argument to itself.
Safe uses: M(I)(42) = 42, M(K)('a') = function.
Warning: M is dangerous, only works with functions expecting functions.
Move to Block 24: Warbler W.
Warbler W (duplicate).
W: lambda f: lambda x: f(x)(x).
Doubling: W(add)(5) = 10, W(add)(7) = 14.
Diagonal: W(eq)(5) = True, uses equality with self.
Move to Block 25: B from SKI derivation.
B = S(KS)K verification.
Definition: B_from_SK = S(K(S))(K).
Tests: B_from_SK(add_one)(double)(5) = 11, B_from_SK(str)(double)(5) = '10'.
Move to Block 26: Z combinator in combinatory style.
Z combinator and factorial/fib via Z.
Z: applicative-order Y with eta-expansion.
Factorial: step and Z create working factorial without def.
Fibonacci: fib_step and Z create working fib.

steps.question: What does print([factorial(n) for n in range(8)]) output?

steps.description: Move to Block 27: The Flock in Practice.
All birds in Python edition with pair and Church numeral examples.
Bird definitions: I, K, S, B, C, W, M, T, V.
KI: K(I) is Church false.
Pairs: V as pair constructor, fst, snd using K and KI.

steps.question: What does print(fst(p), snd(p)) output for p = pair(1)(2)?
